title: Biodiversity of Plants

standard_text: The diversity of plants: bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms; the move from water to land; alternation of generations; reproduction in angiosperms: flowers, pollination, seeds and fruits; the importance of plants. (summary of CAPS Life Sciences, Grade 11, Life Sciences: Biodiversity of plants and reproduction)
meta_desc: Free Grade 11 Life Sciences worksheets (CAPS): bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms, vascular tissue, seeds, pollination and the importance of plants. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Angiosperms have flowers and seeds inside fruits.
key_sub: Gymnosperms have naked seeds in cones.
body_html:
How to think about it

Bryophytes (mosses) have no vascular tissue and need water for fertilisation. Pteridophytes (ferns) have vascular tissue but reproduce by spores. Gymnosperms (pines, cycads) have seeds in cones. Angiosperms (flowering plants) have flowers and their seeds are enclosed in fruits.

Adaptations for life on land include vascular tissue, a waterproof cuticle, stomata, and seeds that do not need water for fertilisation. In angiosperms pollen is carried by wind, insects or birds; after fertilisation the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit.

Example

Which plant group has no vascular tissue?

Mosses

Answer: bryophytes

Example

Which group are cycads?

Seeds in cones

Answer: gymnosperms

Common mistakes

  • Thinking ferns make seeds.
  • Thinking all plants have flowers.
  • Mixing up pollination and fertilisation.

faq.q: Why are seeds an advantage on land?
faq.a: They protect the embryo, store food and can survive dry periods until conditions are good.

faq.q: Why are cycads protected in South Africa?
faq.a: Many species are endangered because they grow slowly and are collected illegally.

items.q: What is the advantage of vascular tissue?
c: water and food can be carried long distances, so plants can grow tall
it lets plants live only in water
items.e: Xylem and phloem support and transport.

items.q: Which algae have the pigment fucoxanthin?
items.e: It gives the olive-green to brown colour.

items.q: Which plant group has seeds that are not enclosed in fruits, usually in cones?
items.e: Gymnosperms: seeds that are not enclosed in fruits, usually in cones.

items.q: Why are seeds an advantage over spores?
c: a seed has an embryo, a food store and a protective coat
items.e: Seeds can stay dormant until conditions are good.

items.q: What is the protonema?
c: the first, alga-like stage of a moss gametophyte
items.e: It grows from a spore.

items.q: Which plant group has flowers, and seeds enclosed in fruits?
items.e: Angiosperms: flowers, and seeds enclosed in fruits.

items.q: What is alternation of generations?
c: a life cycle with a haploid gametophyte stage and a diploid sporophyte stage
a plant that reproduces only asexually
a plant that changes colour each season
items.e: In mosses the gametophyte is dominant; in ferns and seed plants the sporophyte is.

items.q: Which feature describes the bryophytes?
c: vascular tissue, but they reproduce by spores
seeds that are not enclosed in fruits, usually in cones
no vascular tissue, and they need water for fertilisation
flowers, and seeds enclosed in fruits
items.e: Bryophytes: no vascular tissue, and they need water for fertilisation.

items.q: What does the cuticle on a leaf do?
c: it absorbs water from the air
it is a waxy layer that reduces water loss
it carries water up the stem
items.e: It is an adaptation to life on land.

items.q: What is a haplontic life cycle?
c: the sporophyte is only the one-celled zygote; the gametophyte is dominant
items.e: Seen in Volvox, Spirogyra and some Chlamydomonas.

items.q: Which group of plants is described as bryophytes?
c: the first land plants with vascular tissue (xylem and phloem)
flowering plants with seeds enclosed in fruits
the amphibians of the plant kingdom
plants with naked seeds, not enclosed in an ovary
items.e: The amphibians of the plant kingdom: bryophytes.

items.q: Which feature describes the gymnosperms?
c: flowers, and seeds enclosed in fruits
seeds that are not enclosed in fruits, usually in cones
vascular tissue, but they reproduce by spores
no vascular tissue, and they need water for fertilisation
items.e: Gymnosperms: seeds that are not enclosed in fruits, usually in cones.

items.q: What is heterospory?
c: producing two kinds of spores, large megaspores and small microspores
items.e: e.g. Selaginella and Salvinia; a step towards seeds.

items.q: Why is pollen an advantage for seed plants on land?
c: the male gametes can reach the egg without water
items.e: Pollen is carried by wind or animals.

items.q: Which plant group has vascular tissue, but they reproduce by spores?
items.e: Pteridophytes: vascular tissue, but they reproduce by spores.

items.q: Why are mosses small and found in damp places?
c: they have no vascular tissue and need water for fertilisation
items.e: Water must carry the sperm to the egg.

items.e: Pteridophytes: vascular tissue, but they reproduce by spores.

items.q: Which fungi belong to Basidiomycetes?
items.e: Basidiomycetes: mushrooms, bracket fungi and smuts.

items.e: Angiosperms: flowers, and seeds enclosed in fruits.

items.q: In which group is the gametophyte the dominant generation?
items.e: The green moss plant is the gametophyte.

items.q: Is the ovule part of the male or the female part of a flower?
items.e: The stamen (anther and filament) is male; the pistil (stigma, style and ovary) is female.

items.q: A pollen tube grows down the style to the ovule. What happened just before this?
c: Pollen is carried from the anther to the stigma (pollination).
The male reproductive cell joins with the female reproductive cell in the ovule (fertilisation).
The ovule develops into a seed and the ovary develops into a fruit.
The seeds are dispersed and germinate into new plants.
items.e: Pollination → fertilisation → seed and fruit → dispersal → germination.

items.q: Why do sunbirds visit proteas?
c: they drink nectar and carry pollen from flower to flower
they build nests in the flowers
items.e: Birds are important pollinators of proteas.

items.q: What does the filament of a flower do?
c: It receives pollen; it is often sticky.
It contains the ovules and becomes the fruit.
items.e: The filament holds up the anther.

items.q: What does the sepal of a flower do?
c: It is often brightly coloured to attract insects.
It protects the flower when it is a bud.
It contains the ovules and becomes the fruit.
items.e: The sepal protects the flower when it is a bud.

items.q: Which part of a flower becomes the seed?
items.e: The ovary becomes the fruit.

items.q: What does the ovule of a flower do?

items.q: Why are plants important to humans?
c: they provide food, oxygen, medicines, building materials and fuel
they use up all the oxygen
items.e: Many medicines come from indigenous plants.

items.q: How are the seeds or fruits of the rubber tree dispersed?
items.e: Feature of the rubber tree: dry fruit that splits open with a pop. The dry fruit splits open and flings the seeds out.

items.q: Why is double fertilisation so called?
c: two fusions happen in the embryo sac: syngamy and triple fusion
items.e: It is unique to flowering plants.

items.q: Which part of a flower has this job: to attract insects with colour and scent?

items.q: How are the seeds of a coconut usually dispersed?
c: by the wind, with fluffy parachutes
by animals, with hooks that stick to fur
by water, floating to new places
items.e: Seeds are spread away from the parent so the new plants have space, light and water.

by animals that eat the fruit and drop the seeds

items.q: At what stage are pollen grains shed in most angiosperms?
items.e: In about 40% of species they are shed at the 3-celled stage.

items.q: Which term describes this: more than one embryo forms in a seed, as in citrus?
items.e: Polyembryony: more than one embryo forms in a seed, as in citrus.

items.q: Which term describes this: removing the anthers from a bisexual flower before they shed pollen?

items.q: Which term describes this: pollen goes to a flower of a different plant?

items.q: How many nuclei are there in a typical mature embryo sac (Polygonum type)?
items.e: Three antipodals, two synergids, one egg and a central cell with two polar nuclei.

items.q: What is the filiform apparatus?

items.e: It is at the micropylar end.

items.q: What is the outer layer of the pollen grain made of?
